Thesis Chapter 4 Reproduction & validation report RABBIT repository

Robust CLF-QP and
L₁ Adaptive Control

Chapter 3's controller was built from a model of the robot and assumed the model was right. Chapter 4 runs it on a robot the model gets wrong — 30% lighter, 50% heavier, three times heavier, or carrying up to 70 kg it is never told about — and tests two remedies: a robust CLF-QP that defends a worst case, and an L₁ adaptive law that estimates the error and cancels it. Twenty-five steps per run at 1 kHz, and up to 120 in the long-horizon study.

§ 4.0  ·  the setting

Two models, and the gap between them

Chapter 3 had one model. Chapter 4 has two: the simulation integrates the true dynamics f, g, and every controller is built from the nominal dynamics f̃, g̃. The split is structural rather than a convention — ch4_control calls the input–output linearization with its model argument empty, which pins it to the nominal model, and no code path leads from a controller to the true dynamics. Set p.uncertainty to zero and Chapter 4 reduces to Chapter 3 exactly; ch4_test_model asserts it at zero error.

Applying the nominal pre-control u = ũ_ff + (L_g̃L_f̃y)⁻¹μ to the true plant turns Chapter 3's clean double integrator into

ÿ = μ + Δ₁ + Δ₂ μ (4.3) Δ₁ = L_f²y − L_gL_f y · (L_g̃L_f̃ y)⁻¹ · L_f̃²y (4.4) Δ₂ = L_gL_f y · (L_g̃L_f̃ y)⁻¹ − I

The two terms fail in different ways. Δ₁ ≠ 0 removes the equilibrium: the tracking error cannot reach zero however hard the controller pushes. Δ₂ ≠ 0 means the controller's authority is wrong, and at ‖Δ₂‖ ≥ 1 the model can cancel or reverse the intended effect.

The chapter's own perturbation is unusually clean

For a uniform mass and inertia scale s, the stance KKT system splits exactly: the drift acceleration does not depend on s, and the input acceleration scales as 1/s. With no approximation at all,

Δ₂ = (1/s − 1) · I exactly isotropic Δ₁ = −(1/s − 1) · L_f̃²y exactly proportional to the output drift (both verified to ~1e−13)
  • The thesis's scalar Δ₂ model is exact here, not an approximation. Remark 4.5 assumes Δ₂ = d₂I to reduce the min–max to two linear inequalities; for a uniform scale that assumption is simply true.
  • ‖Δ₂‖ < 1 requires s > 0.5. Below half the nominal mass no worst-case design can help: the bound itself contains a model that cancels the control.
  • Δ₁ grows away from the orbit. A bound valid on a neighborhood is 4.9× the bound valid on the orbit — 1140.6 against 232.6 on posture_195. That gap is §4.1.4's "unnecessarily aggressive" limitation, with a number on it.

A load at the hip is not a small mass scale

A point mass changes the mass matrix non-uniformly. Along the orbit, loads of 23–70 kg give ‖Δ₂‖ = 1.99–2.72, of which the isotropic part is only 0.19–0.30. The eigenvalues of I + Δ₂ stay real and positive (as low as 0.30), so no direction reverses — but every load sits outside anything the robust law's bound can cover. That is why the load study, like the thesis, leaves the robust law out.

§ 4.1  ·  defending the worst case

Robust CLF-QP: hold the bound, then stop it chattering

Under uncertainty V̇ = L_fV + L_gV·Δ₁ + L_gV(I + Δ₂)μ. The maximum over the Δ₁ ball, D₁‖L_gV‖, does not involve μ, so it folds into Chapter 3's residual; under the scalar model the Δ₂ maximum becomes two linear inequalities. The least-norm solution is closed-form:

a = ψ + D₁‖L_gV‖, ψ = L_fV + (c₃/ε)V μ* = − a · L_gVᵀ / ((1 − D₂) ‖L_gV‖²) when a > 0, otherwise 0 (4.12)

With D₁ = D₂ = 0 it is Chapter 3's law exactly (3.4e−13 in the test suite), and 1 − D₂ > 0 is the precise form of Remark 4.3's "within this region" — past it the code reports the QP infeasible instead of dividing by a non-positive number.

The exact law is sliding-mode control, and a 1 kHz hold makes it chatter

Near the orbit ψ is O(‖η‖²) while D₁‖L_gV‖ is O(‖η‖), so μ* tends to a correction of fixed size M = D₁/(1 − D₂) ≈ 574 along a unit vector that flips every time the state crosses L_gV = 0. Held for 1 ms it cannot slide: one sample moves L_gV by 0.029 and overshoots whatever was left. Over the first three steps the torque actually held changed by a median of 253 / 573 / 481 Nm per sample in Cases I–III.

p.rclf.boundary_layer = κ replaces the unit vector with a saturation of width φ = κ(1 + D₂)φ_T. One held sample inside the layer multiplies L_gV by, at worst, 1 − 1/κ over the bound — which gives κ its units: above ½ the sampled loop converges, and from 1 it converges without overshoot.

Measured at the earlier ε = 0.35; nothing in the layer's algebra depends on ε. At κ = 0.33 the predicted per-sample multiplier is −1.0 / −0.33 / −1.86 for the three true input gains, and only the case below −1 chattered. A thicker layer trades tracking for margin; κ = 1 is the thinnest that cannot overshoot anywhere in the bound.

The price of a sampled controller: ultimate boundedness

Inside the layer the worst case may exceed (4.11) by at most D₁φ/4, so V̇ ≤ −(c₃/ε)V + D₁φ/4. The thesis's "tracking errors converging to zero" needs continuous control; an implementation that holds its control for a sample gets a bounded error instead. Inside the layer the correction also stops depending on D₁, so the "more robustness costs more μ" price is capped by the sample period.

The contact rows are advisory, and still necessary

The constrained form (4.13) adds a torque box, a friction cone and a normal-force floor. The box is exact under uncertainty, because u is applied verbatim. The contact rows are not: they constrain the nominal model's prediction of the contact force (Remark 4.4). Stripping them is still not physical. With the exact law and no floor, the true stance foot was pulled into the ground on 17 / 38 / 42% of samples in Cases I–III (min Fz −1621 / −3220 / −3543 N); with the rows on it stayed at ≥ 23 N. Even with the boundary layer, 25 steps at ×0.7 without the rows put 1.8% of samples below zero.

Cases I–III over 25 steps

Three controllers, as in §4.1.4: A is Chapter 3's min-norm CLF-QP, B the same with the torque box and contact rows (friction and normal-force floor), and C the robust law with the same box and rows. Every cell reads steps · valid steps · max‖η‖ · min Fz, with Fz the true normal force. A run is valid up to its first sample with Fz ≤ 0 (lift-off) or |Fx|/Fz > 0.4 (slip): the simulator pins the stance foot, so step count alone scores unwalkable runs as walking.

One actuator rating for every controller and case: 556 Nm, 1.25 × the heaviest feedforward in the design envelope, so no box carries knowledge of the perturbation it is about to meet. The thesis's 60 / 80 / 150 Nm, set for a 32 kg robot, are 12–41% of what A draws on this 74 kg model, and both constrained laws fell in every case with them. A negative min Fz means the ground had to pull the foot down: those steps are not realizable. The simulator keeps the stance foot attached, modelling neither lift-off nor slip, so such a run still completes its steps, and the valid-step column is what scores it. D₁ and D₂ are still measured from the perturbation itself, which no controller has in practice; the box no longer is. The robust and L₁ sections now run at the same 556 Nm budget and are comparable.

Nothing falls within 25 steps at ε = 0.20; validity is what separates the rows. The baselines reach max‖η‖ 14–17, their step times wander over 0.184–0.346 s against a nominal 0.2733 s, and neither has a single valid step at ×0.7: A drives the normal force to −1734 N, while B keeps it positive but demands μ up to 20, fifty times the coefficient its own rows are written with. Even with a perfect model A slips in step 2. The robust law holds max‖η‖ at 4.24 / 4.34, keeps its step times within 0.264–0.284 s and the true normal force at ≥ 90 N and ≥ 23 N, and walks all 25 steps validly at ×1 and ×1.5 — but only 5 valid steps at ×0.7. The larger box also changes the law itself: at ×1 its max‖η‖ went 1.13 → 2.85 and its peak torque 195 → 371 Nm.

Remarks 4.6 and 4.7 hold early, not in the long run

The steady error no longer grows with the perturbation — at one box the largest plateau is Case I's, 9.05, against 5.27 / 5.64 / 1.88 — gracefully, and even the 60-step maxima stay below what the baselines reach within 25 steps. With a perfect model the robust law settles at max‖η‖ ≈ 9 against the plain CLF-QP's 0.25: Remark 4.7's advantage, tighter tracking when the worst case is not happening, is gone by step 10 and does not return within 60.

Not reproduced: the slowdown to a stop

The thesis reports Case IV walking that "slows down after several steps to a complete stop", and attributes it to an unstable orbit. Here C averages 1.576 m/s over the first three steps and 1.541 m/s over the last five, and a 120-step run is still at 1.563 m/s. If the thesis's Case IV is also a uniform mass scale — which this report has not checked — the explanation cannot apply to this model: a uniform mass scale leaves the hybrid zero dynamics exactly invariant, and posture_195's are stable (δ²_zero = 0.746). What does happen past step 25 is that the degradation stops being slight at this box: max‖η‖ holds near 1.9 and the V plateau near 0.17 out to step 120, the lowest of the four cases. The old drift to 10.9 belonged to the much larger per-case box, not to the scale.

§ 4.2  ·  estimate, then cancel

L₁ adaptive control: four fixes before it holds

The robust law pays its worst-case price whether or not the worst case happens. L₁ estimates the uncertainty and cancels it, so a perfect model costs nothing. The applied input splits as μ = μ₁ + μ₂: μ₁ is Chapter 3's CLF-QP itself — a nonlinear reference model with no closed form — and μ₂ = −C(s)θ̂ cancels the estimate θ̂ = α̂‖η‖ + β̂. Unlike anything in Chapter 3, the controller has state: twenty entries, holding the state predictor, the two estimates and the filter output.

Run as §4.2 writes it, the controller does not reproduce its own claim on this robot. Over 25 steps it tracks no better than its reference model under either perturbation, falls at ×1.5 in step 14, and needs the ground to pull the foot down on 11–14% of samples. Four changes make it hold. Each is an option in p.l1, and the thesis form stays one setting away.

1 · The predictor is driven by what the plant received

The thesis predictor (4.19) runs its own copy of the reference model, η̂̇ = Fη̂ + Gμ̂₁ + G(μ₂ + θ̂), with μ̂₁ a second CLF-QP solved on η̂. The step from (4.24) to (4.28) needs μ̂₁(η̂) − μ₁(η) to decrease P_ε along η̃, but the two QPs only guarantee a decrease along η and along η̂ separately, and the min-norm law is nonlinear. The mismatch forces η̃ exactly as a model error would, and the adaptation absorbs it: at ε = 0.20, θ̂ overshoots θ 7.2× at ×0.7 and 2.0× at ×1.5. The standard L₁ predictor instead uses the input the plant actually received,

η̂̇ = Fη + G(μ + θ̂) − a(η̂ − η) ⇒ η̃̇ = −a η̃ + G θ̃ exactly, with no reference model in it

so P = I, the law adapts on the velocity prediction error, the β channel closes the loop s² + as + Γ, and the second QP per call disappears.

2 · The sampled advance sees the plant's inputs

The thesis advance froze η across each 1 ms period while letting μ₂ move with the filter; the plant saw the opposite. The advance now holds the applied μ and reads η at both ends of the period, which stays causal because η is sampled at t_(k+1) before the next control is computed. On a tracking double integrator this estimates θ to 1e−15 relative error, where freezing η leaves a 2.5% bias. After each period the estimates are also returned to their projection balls: projection bounds them only in continuous time, and before that clamp θ̂ once reached 1e7.

3 · The constrained law bounds the torque it applies

§4.2.3 boxes μ₁ alone and adds no contact rows, so μ₂ reaches the joints outside every constraint. With p.l1.constrain_applied, μ₂ enters the QP as a known offset: the cost and the CLF row still act on μ₁, while the box and the friction and normal-force rows bound the total torque. Because the box now carries the whole robot, it scales with it, u_max · max(1, s): a 1.5× robot needs 293 Nm of feedforward alone, above a rating of 556 Nm, which covers the 293 Nm a ×1.5 robot's feedforward alone needs.

4 · The adaptation is normalized for the sampled loop

The loop from prediction error to estimates runs at about √(Γ + Γ_α‖η‖²) rad/s, so it speeds up as tracking degrades. After a bad footstrike, at ‖η‖ = 13, it reaches 4.1 rad per 1 ms sample — faster than a 1 kHz controller can realize. Both adaptation laws are therefore divided by

m² = max(1, (Γ + Γ_α‖η‖²) / (ρ/Δt)²), ρ = 0.75 rad per sample p.l1.normalized_rate

which holds the loop at ρ rad per sample and leaves the law untouched while the loop is slower. θ̂ itself is unchanged. The Lyapunov argument survives in weakened form: with the prediction error weighted by 1/m² the cross terms still cancel, but the bound on the prediction error loosens by the factor m, and holds only while m² decays slower than e^(−2at) — which a footstrike can break. The long-horizon section below is why this fix exists, and why ρ is 0.75.

The italic row is §4.2 as written — thesis predictor, Γ = 1e4, box on μ₁ alone — from ch4_l1_2026-09-13_18-26-49. Normalization moves the table only slightly: with the first three fixes alone, B read 4.81 · −362 N at ×0.7 and 2.17 at ×1.5, and C 4.58 and 4.51. At ×1 it never engages.

With a perfect model, L₁ is at least the CLF-QP. Its max‖η‖ is 0.14 against 0.25, and its CLF between impacts is about four times lower. The estimate is not quite zero (‖θ̂‖ ≤ 9), because the 1 kHz hold makes the output acceleration drift within each period, and L₁ cancels part of that intersample error. In continuous time the identity is exact, and the test suite checks it there: with no model error nothing adapts, to machine precision.

The steps complete under either perturbation — the contact does not. Both laws walk all 25 steps with max‖η‖ 2.4–6.1 against the baseline's 14.5–16.5, keep step times near nominal, and hold the per-step CLF peak nearly flat where the robust law's grows. At ×1.5 l1_con walks all 25 steps validly (Fz ≥ 91 N, μ ≤ 0.27). At ×0.7 no law has a single valid step: clfqp and l1 drive the normal force to −1734 N and −220 N, and l1_con keeps Fz ≥ 23 N but demands μ up to 1.58, four times μ_s. Its contact rows are written on the nominal model, so they bound the friction the controller believes it needs, not what the true, lighter robot needs.

§ 4.2.4  ·  Fig. 4.11  ·  an unknown load

Carrying an unknown load: 25 steps at any load, valid contact only to about a third of body weight

The robot carries a mass at the hip that no controller knows about: redrawn every step from 0–70 kg (Fig. 4.11a), or fixed at 23 / 35 / 46 kg (Fig. 4.11b). Those are the thesis's 0–30 kg and 10 / 15 / 20 kg scaled by this robot's mass, ×74/32, so each load is the same share of body weight. Two design choices, both measured:

  • A second baseline. Besides §4.2.4's three controllers, the study runs clfqp_con with the same box and contact rows as l1_con. Under load the unconstrained CLF-QP draws 2–3.5× l1_con's peak torque, so a comparison against it alone cannot say whether the adaptation or the torque is doing the work.
  • The box. 1.25 × the loaded robot's own feedforward peak along the orbit — for a uniform scale, exactly the L₁ preset's rule. Sized by mass ratio instead, l1_con fell within three steps at 46 and 70 kg. The box is built from the loaded robot's feedforward, i.e. from the load no controller is told about: the budget is equal for all, but chosen knowing the load.

l1_con's negative normal forces are single samples: 1, 3 and 2 of about 15 000. Plain l1 asks the ground to pull on 4.7% of samples at 35 kg and 10.5% at 46 kg, and under the random load falls in step 15 — the first step after the load drops from 60 to 12 kg.

By step count the adaptation walks; by validity, only at the lightest load. l1_con completes all 25 steps of every case, the random 0–70 kg draw included — the thesis's claim. clfqp_con, with the same box and rows, falls under the random load and at 35 and 46 kg. But scored against its contact, l1_con is valid for all 25 steps only at 23 kg — about a third of body weight, where clfqp_con is too — dropping to 7 valid steps at 35 kg, 2 at 46 kg and 15 under the random load, with the true normal force going negative in the two heaviest cases. So L₁ carries an unknown load with a valid contact up to roughly a third of body weight, not 94% of it. The thesis form is worse again: measured separately at the same boxes, it reached max‖η‖ of about 27 at 46 kg and about 103 at 70 kg, with θ̂ overshooting 2–4×, and its constrained law fell in step 3 at 70 kg.

What normalization costs inside those 25 steps

At the one rating the cost is small: l1_con's worst step under the random load is 9.79 and its true normal force stays at ≥ 3 N. What normalization buys is in the long horizon, not here. At the fixed loads its worst step moves by less than 10% either way (2.41 / 4.86 / 5.22 without). Plain l1 gets worse at 35 kg, 5.06 → 6.98. What normalization buys is on the long runs, two sections down.

Past the thesis's horizon  ·  60–120 steps

Why L₁ fell in the long runs, and what fixed most of it

The thesis stops at 25 steps. Extended to 60 (120 for plain l1 at ×1.5) with the first three fixes alone, l1_con held every mass scale, but plain l1 at ×1.5 fell in step 76, and under the random load l1_con fell in all four draw sequences tried — steps 43, 33, 55 and 57 — where the unconstrained CLF-QP walked all 60 steps of each.

The drift is real, but it is a symptom. θ̂ = α̂‖η‖ + β̂ is redundant: while ‖η‖ stays near a value, every split of θ between α̂ and β̂ predicts equally well, so nothing holds the split. Over long runs the two estimates drift into near-opposite directions (median cosine −0.91 at ×0.7, −0.95 at ×1.5) and α̂ presses its projection bound. Leaking α̂ back to zero made things worse, not better.

The falls are the estimator loop outrunning the sample rate. Three of the five falls were re-simulated sample by sample, and each starts within a few milliseconds of a footstrike that leaves ‖η‖ at 12–14. There the loop runs at about 4100 rad/s — 4.1 rad per sample, past the RK4 advance's own stability limit of about 2.8 — and within 1–3 samples θ̂ reaches 2700–2900 against a true θ of 30–300. The adaptive torque swamps the QP, and the step collapses. ch4_test_l1 check 10 isolates that loop at ‖η‖ = 13.

ρ was picked on those nine runs, so the candidates were rerun on six further 0–70 kg sequences, p.load_seed 4–9, each l1_con over 60 steps:

The long-horizon screens measure max‖η‖ on every third solver point and were run as scratch studies; their numbers are recorded in docs/CH4_UNCERTAINTY.md §5a rather than saved under Results/.
  • Across all fifteen long runs, ρ = 0.75 falls once, against nine without normalization and four with the cap. That total mixes the nine runs ρ was picked on with six test runs; on the six fresh sequences, one fall against two (ρ = 1) is not a distinguishable difference, and ρ = 0.75 has the largest excursion among completed runs (49.8). The one fall is seed 6, which the unnormalized law walks and which brings down all three 1 kHz limits tried on it. Both kinds of limit slow the estimator most when the error is largest — which is also when a changed load has to be learned. That is the likely reason; it has not been checked sample by sample.
  • What survives is not always clean. Two of the new sequences pass through excursions to max‖η‖ 20–50 at ρ = 0.75 and still walk.
  • Only the faster loop is both safe and flat. At 0.5 ms, with neither limit, the law fell once in twelve runs and never exceeded max‖η‖ 16 on the new sequences.

Adopted: ρ = 0.75, at 1 kHz

With it, plain l1 at ×1.5 walks all 120 steps at max‖η‖ 2.0–2.9 per block, l1_con walks all four original random-load sequences and five of the six new ones, and the 46 kg run still holds 60 steps. l1_con at ×1.5 no longer settles the way it did without normalization: 4.8 in steps 1–10, 2.2–2.4 through step 40, then 3.5 and 5.5. The §4.2.4 and Fig. 4.11 tables above are the reruns with ρ = 0.75.

Caveats  ·  measured, not assumed

Three things worth being explicit about

1. Every guarantee is continuous-time; the controller is not

Both remedies needed a fix that exists only because control is held for a sample: the boundary layer, which turns the robust law's convergence into ultimate boundedness, and normalization, which keeps L₁'s estimator slower than the sample rate. Even with a perfect model the hold kicks every impact:

Tracking error after the first footstrike, perfect modelposture_195 · ‖η⁺‖
Control period‖η⁺‖ after step 1Status
1 ms  default0.242visible kick
0.5 ms0.123halved
0.2 ms0.049O(dt)
continuous1.7e−4on the orbit
The pre-impact error is small, 6.8e−3 at 1 ms; the impact map amplifies it about 35×. That is the jump every perfect-model curve shows at each footstrike — the discretization, not the model.

2. Remark 4.4, measured

The friction rows hold the nominal prediction at μ ≤ 0.4. Over 25 steps the true demand is p95 0.22 / 0.12 / 0.26 in Cases I–III, with peaks of 0.25 and 0.39 in Cases I–II — and at ×0.7 it briefly reaches 1.49: a momentary slip the controller cannot see, which is exactly the gap Remark 4.4 warns about. Contact forces in this report always come from the true model; computed from the controller's own model, as Chapter 3's analysis did, they would be off by 50% at ×1.5.

3. The ×1.5 results are tuning, not margin

The predictor-rate sweep, the ρ window with edges at 0.5 and 1.5 each falling twice in nine runs, and a single seed that defeats every 1 kHz limit all say the same thing: at mass scale 1.5 and under a load redrawn every step, L₁ at 1 kHz works where it has been tuned to work. The sweeps are reported so that claim can be judged rather than taken.

Verification  ·  ch4_test_all

What the test suite actually asserts

The order is the order to debug in: the model split first, then each controller's algebra, then the behaviour the chapter claims.

Full suite — 50 checks, 0 failures, 9.8 sMATLAB R2021b · run 2026-09-14
ModuleChecksWhat it pins downSharpest result
ch4_test_model17 the nominal model is Chapter 3's; the exact Δ structure under a mass scale; the load's mass matrix, gravity and impact map; forces under a per-step load Δ₂ == (1/s − 1)I, err 2.1e−13
ch4_test_rclf14 the closed form, the RES condition over sampled balls of Δ, the box, infeasibility at D₂ ≥ 1, and the boundary layer's guarantee, cap and chatter held-torque jumps 1000 → 0 per 1000 samples
ch4_test_l119 projection, both predictors' error dynamics, the filter, the perfect-model identity, the rows on the applied torque, the sampled advance, and the estimator loop at a post-impact error at ‖η‖ = 13: diverges as written, settles normalized
Two checks guard against silent wrongness rather than loud wrongness. baseline is NOT robust confirms that Chapter 3's law violates the robust condition on 294 of 1200 sampled uncertainties — otherwise the robust tests could pass vacuously. And the two identities that tie Chapter 4 back to Chapter 3 are asserted, not claimed: with D₁ = D₂ = 0 the robust law is the CLF-QP (3.4e−13), and with no model error L₁ adapts nothing, to zero.

What carries forward

What this hands to the later chapters

The machinery generalizes: a structural split between the model the robot obeys and the model the controller holds, the Δ terms computed from both, per-step loads, and contact forces always taken from the true model. Every later controller that is built from a model inherits the question this chapter asks of it.

Limitations to carry with it

  • Contact constraints are only as good as the model. Every friction and normal-force row here constrains a prediction, and the true friction demand reached 1.49 against a 0.4 row. The thesis returns to contact constraints in Chapter 8; nothing in Chapter 4 makes them robust.
  • The robust bound cannot cover a realistic load. ‖Δ₂‖ is 2.0–2.7 for a hip load, outside any bound the robust law can use, and even inside its bound the law pays a steady error with a perfect model.
  • L₁ at 1 kHz needs sample-rate-aware design, and still falls on 1 of 6 fresh load sequences. The adopted ρ sits in a window measured on this robot; a faster loop is the cleaner fix where the hardware allows it.
  • Chapter 5's barrier functions are model-based too. A robust or adaptive ECBF is the natural composition of the two chapters, and neither attempts it.

Appendix  ·  reproducing this

Running it

% everything: bounds, the three sweeps, the load study, figures, GIFs
ch4_main

% the full test suite (~10 s)
ch4_test_all

% one stage at a time
ch4_main('presets', {'robust'})
ch4_main('presets', {'case4'}, 'animate', false)
ch4_main('presets', {'l1'},    'animate', false)
ch4_main('presets', {'load'},  'animate', false)

% any ch4_params field, by dotted name
ch4_main('rclf.boundary_layer', 0)          % the exact robust law, chatter included
ch4_main('l1.normalized_rate', 0)           % L1 without fix 4
ch4_main('l1.predictor', 'thesis', 'l1.constrain_applied', false, 'l1.Gamma', 1e4)

ch4_main first refuses a gait that is not a periodic orbit of the dynamics currently on the path: a gait file does not record which dynamics it was solved on, and Chapter 4 once ran for ten days on one that no longer was. It then measures Δ₁ and Δ₂ along a nominal rollout and adopts 1.2× the maxima as the robust bounds, unless they are passed in. The full study takes about ten minutes at 1 kHz, plus about two for Case IV and four for the load study.
